hook: Mortgage literally means death pledge.
facts: The word comes from old French.
Mort means death, and gage means a promise.
The deal dies when the loan is paid off, or when the land is lost.

hook: Tanks got their name from a lie.
facts: In World War One, Britain built a secret armored machine.
To keep it hidden, factory workers were told they were making water tanks.
The cover story stuck, and we still call them tanks today.

hook: Jeans and denim are named after two cities.
facts: Denim comes from serge de Nimes, a strong cloth from the French city of Nimes.
Jeans comes from the old French name for Genoa, in Italy.
Sailors from Genoa wore trousers made of a tough cotton cloth.

hook: The tuxedo is named after a rich neighborhood.
facts: In the eighteen eighties, rich families in New York had a club called Tuxedo Park.
Some young men there started wearing short dinner jackets instead of long tailcoats.
People named the jacket after the place, and the word went around the world.

hook: The bikini is named after a nuclear test site.
facts: In nineteen forty-six, America tested atomic bombs at Bikini Atoll in the Pacific.
A few days later, a French designer showed a tiny new swimsuit.
He named it after the atoll, hoping it would be just as explosive.

hook: The cardigan is named after a war commander.
facts: The Earl of Cardigan led British soldiers in the Crimean War.
His men wore warm knitted jackets that opened at the front.
He led a famous and disastrous cavalry charge, but his sweater won the war of fashion.

hook: Sideburns are named after a general's face.
facts: Ambrose Burnside was a general in the American Civil War.
He had a famous style: thick hair on his cheeks, but a shaved chin.
People called them burnsides, and over time the word flipped into sideburns.

hook: The leotard is named after a flying acrobat.
facts: Jules Leotard was a French acrobat in the eighteen hundreds.
He invented the flying trapeze act, jumping from one swing to another.
He wore a tight one piece suit, and a famous song was written about him.

hook: Shampoo comes from a word for massage.
facts: The word comes from Hindi, and it means to press or knead.
In the eighteen hundreds, an Indian businessman opened a bath house in England.
He offered head massages called shampooing, and the word moved to hair soap.

hook: Alcohol was once the name of eye makeup.
facts: The word comes from Arabic al kuhl, a fine black powder.
People wore it around their eyes, and it was made by heating minerals.
Later the word meant any pure essence, and finally the spirit in your drink.

hook: Algebra once meant fixing broken bones.
facts: The word comes from the Arabic al jabr, which means putting broken parts back together.
A Baghdad scholar used it in the title of a famous math book.
In old Spain, an algebrista was also a man who set broken bones.

hook: Checkmate comes from Persian words about a king.
facts: Chess came to Europe from Persia, through the Arab world.
In Persian, shah means king.
Shah mat means the king is helpless, and it became checkmate.

hook: Jumbo was the name of one elephant.
facts: In the eighteen hundreds, Jumbo was a giant African elephant at the London Zoo.
Children rode on his back, and he became a superstar.
When he was sold to an American circus, his name became the word for anything huge.

hook: Hello was made popular by the telephone.
facts: When the telephone was invented, people did not know how to answer it.
Alexander Graham Bell wanted everyone to say ahoy, like sailors.
Thomas Edison pushed for hello instead, and his word won.

hook: Lunatic comes from the word for moon.
facts: Luna means moon in Latin.
For centuries, people believed the full moon could drive people mad.
So a lunatic was literally someone touched by the moon.

hook: A companion is someone you share bread with.
facts: The word comes from Latin.
Com means with, and panis means bread.
So your companion is, word for word, the person you break bread with.

hook: Vaccine comes from the word for cow.
facts: In seventeen ninety-six, a doctor noticed milkmaids rarely caught smallpox.
They had already caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows.
He used cowpox to protect people, and named it after vacca, Latin for cow.

hook: Trivia means three roads.
facts: In Latin, tri means three, and via means road.
Where three roads met, people stopped and chatted about small things.
So trivia became the word for little facts nobody really needs.

hook: Deadline was once a line you could not cross.
facts: In a prison camp during the American Civil War, guards marked a line inside the fence.
Any prisoner who crossed it could be shot.
Later newspapers borrowed the word for the time a story must be finished.

hook: Spam emails are named after a comedy sketch.
facts: In a nineteen seventy comedy sketch, a cafe served spam with every dish.
A group of Vikings kept singing spam over and over, drowning out everyone.
Early internet users said junk messages did the same, and the name stuck.

hook: The word guy comes from a man who failed.
facts: In sixteen oh five, Guy Fawkes tried to blow up the English Parliament.
Every year after, people burned straw dolls of him called guys.
A guy came to mean a badly dressed man, and later, any man at all.

hook: Silly once meant blessed.
facts: In Old English, the word meant happy or lucky.
Over the centuries it shifted to innocent, then to simple.
Today it just means foolish, a long way from blessed.

hook: Girl once meant any child.
facts: In the Middle Ages, a girl could be a boy or a girl.
It simply meant a young person.
Boys were sometimes called knave girls, and only later did the word mean a female child.

hook: Bankrupt means broken bench.
facts: In old Italy, money lenders worked at benches in the market.
The Italian word for bench was banca, which gave us bank.
When a lender failed, his bench was broken, banca rotta, and he was bankrupt.

hook: The pupil of your eye means little doll.
facts: Look closely into someone's eye, and you see a tiny version of yourself.
The Romans called that dark center pupilla, which means little doll.
School pupils got the same word, because they were also small people.

hook: Window means wind eye.
facts: The word comes from the Old Norse language of the Vikings.
Vindauga means wind eye.
Early houses had just a hole in the roof or wall, where wind and light came in.

hook: Dandelion means lion's tooth.
facts: The name comes from the French dent de lion.
Look at the leaves: they have sharp, pointed edges.
Someone thought they looked like the teeth of a lion, and the name stuck.

hook: Hippopotamus means river horse.
facts: The name comes from ancient Greek.
Hippo means horse, and potamus means river.
Hippos are not related to horses at all; their closest living relatives are whales.

hook: Daisy means the eye of the day.
facts: The old English name was the day's eye.
A daisy opens its petals in the morning, showing its yellow center.
At night it closes up again, like an eye going to sleep.

hook: Nachos are named after a real man.
facts: In nineteen forty-three, a group of women walked into a restaurant in Mexico, near Texas.
The cook was gone, so the waiter, Ignacio Anaya, made a snack from what he had.
He put cheese and peppers on fried tortilla chips, and named them after his nickname, Nacho.

hook: The chocolate chip cookie was sold for chocolate.
facts: In the nineteen thirties, Ruth Wakefield ran an inn in Massachusetts.
She chopped a chocolate bar into her cookie dough, and they became famous.
She let a chocolate company print the recipe, and they gave her free chocolate for life.

hook: The first chocolate was a bitter spicy drink.
facts: In Mexico, the Maya and Aztecs drank chocolate long before Europe knew it.
They mixed ground cocoa beans with water, corn and chili peppers.
It was cold, foamy and bitter, and sugar was only added much later in Europe.

hook: Chili con carne is from Texas, not Mexico.
facts: The dish grew up in San Antonio in the eighteen hundreds.
Women called chili queens sold it from street stands in the city squares.
Many Mexicans see it as an American food.

hook: Pepper was once used to pay rent.
facts: In the Middle Ages, black pepper came from far away and was very expensive.
People used peppercorns to pay rent, taxes and even wedding gifts.
Today, in English law, a peppercorn rent means a tiny price, almost nothing.

hook: Pineapple eats you while you eat it.
facts: Pineapples contain a substance that breaks down protein.
Your tongue and cheeks are made of protein too.
That is why your mouth tingles after eating a lot, and the feeling goes away once your mouth heals.

hook: Sushi rice was once thrown away.
facts: The first sushi was a way to keep fish from going bad.
Fish was packed in rice and left to ferment for months.
Then people ate the fish and threw the rice in the bin.

hook: Instant noodles were invented in a backyard shed.
facts: After World War Two, Momofuku Ando saw long lines for noodle soup in Japan.
In a small shed, he tried for a year to make noodles you could cook in minutes.
The trick was frying them, an idea he got from watching his wife make tempura.

hook: A smell once shut down the British Parliament.
facts: In the summer of eighteen fifty-eight, London was very hot.
The river Thames was full of sewage, and the smell became unbearable.
Lawmakers soaked their curtains in chemicals, then finally paid for a modern sewer system.

hook: A war once started because of a pig.
facts: In eighteen fifty-nine, America and Britain both claimed one small island.
An American farmer shot a British company's pig that was eating his potatoes.
Both sides sent soldiers and warships, but the only casualty of the whole war was the pig.

hook: Two Italian cities went to war over a bucket.
facts: In thirteen twenty-five, soldiers from Modena sneaked into Bologna.
They stole a wooden bucket from a well in the city.
A battle followed with thousands of soldiers, and Modena still keeps the bucket.

hook: Tutankhamun had a dagger from outer space.
facts: The young pharaoh was buried with a dagger made of iron.
In his time, iron was rare, and Egyptians did not know how to smelt it.
Scientists tested the metal, and it came from a meteorite that fell from the sky.

hook: Millions of men share one ancestor, Genghis Khan.
facts: Genghis Khan built the largest land empire in history.
Scientists studied the genes of men across Asia.
About one in two hundred men in the world may be his descendant.

hook: Isaac Newton hunted fake money makers.
facts: Late in life, Newton was put in charge of England's money.
He went undercover in bars and disguised himself to catch criminals.
He collected proof and sent the most famous fake money maker to be hanged.

hook: Charles Darwin ate the animals he studied.
facts: At university, Darwin was part of a club that ate strange animals.
On his famous trip, he searched for a rare bird in South America.
He finally found it, after he had already eaten it for dinner.

hook: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive.
facts: Marie Curie spent her life studying radioactive elements.
She often carried radium around in her pockets.
Her notebooks are kept in lead boxes, and visitors must sign a form to read them.

hook: Benjamin Franklin invented swim fins as a boy.
facts: Franklin loved swimming when he was young.
At about eleven, he made wooden paddles to wear on his hands to swim faster.
Centuries later, he was put in the swimming hall of fame.

hook: Mark Twain was born and died with a comet.
facts: Halley's comet flew past Earth in eighteen thirty-five, the year Twain was born.
He said he came in with the comet and expected to go out with it.
The comet came back in nineteen ten, and Twain died the day after it got closest to the Sun.

hook: Agatha Christie once vanished for eleven days.
facts: In nineteen twenty-six, the famous crime writer disappeared from her home.
Thousands of people and police searched for her across England.
She was found in a hotel, staying under the name of her husband's girlfriend.

hook: A famous children's author was a secret spy.
facts: Before he wrote books for children, Roald Dahl was a fighter pilot.
During World War Two, he was sent to Washington.
There he went to parties and quietly passed secrets back to Britain.

hook: James Bond was named after a bird expert.
facts: Ian Fleming wanted the most boring name possible for his spy.
On his shelf was a book about birds of the Caribbean.
The author was a real man named James Bond, and Fleming took his name.

hook: Green Eggs and Ham was written for a bet.
facts: A publisher bet Dr Seuss fifty dollars that he could not write a book with only fifty different words.
Dr Seuss took the bet and wrote Green Eggs and Ham.
It became one of the best selling children's books ever, and the publisher never paid.

hook: A Roman emperor won a race he never finished.
facts: Emperor Nero entered the chariot race at the Olympic Games.
He fell out of his chariot and did not finish the race.
The judges still declared him the winner.

hook: San Marino is the oldest republic in the world.
facts: San Marino is a tiny country inside Italy.
Its story says it was founded in the year three hundred and one by a stonemason.
It has kept its own government for more than seventeen centuries.

hook: One country is ruled by a French president.
facts: Andorra is a small country between France and Spain.
It has two princes who rule it together.
One is a Spanish bishop, and the other is the president of France.

hook: One country moved the calendar to be first.
facts: Kiribati is made of islands spread on both sides of the date line.
So part of the country was a whole day behind the other part.
In nineteen ninety-five, it moved the line, and now it is the first country to see the New Year.

hook: One island changes country every six months.
facts: Pheasant Island sits in a river between France and Spain.
Since sixteen fifty-nine, the two countries have shared it.
It belongs to Spain for six months, then France for six months, again and again.

hook: The loneliest island has no airport and one village.
facts: Tristan da Cunha is in the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean.
Around two hundred and fifty people live in its only village.
There is no airport, so the trip by boat from South Africa takes about a week.

hook: One lake in Australia is bright pink.
facts: Lake Hillier sits on an island off the coast of Western Australia.
Next to the blue ocean, its water is a strong bubblegum pink.
The color comes from tiny salt loving algae, and the water is safe to touch.

hook: One river turns five different colors.
facts: Cano Cristales is a river in Colombia.
For a few months each year, a water plant on its bed turns bright red.
With yellow sand, green moss and blue water, people call it the river of five colors.

hook: A desert crater has been on fire for decades.
facts: Around nineteen seventy-one, Soviet engineers drilled for gas in Turkmenistan.
The ground collapsed, and they set the gas on fire, hoping it would burn out in days.
It is still burning, and people call it the Door to Hell.

hook: Angel Falls is named after a pilot.
facts: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall in the world.
In the nineteen thirties, an American pilot named Jimmie Angel flew over it.
He later landed his plane on top, got stuck in the mud, and walked down for days.

hook: Rocks in one desert move by themselves.
facts: In Death Valley, heavy stones leave long tracks across a dry lake bed.
For decades, nobody saw them move.
Then cameras caught it: thin sheets of ice and light wind push them slowly across the mud.

hook: America bought Alaska for two cents an acre.
facts: In eighteen sixty-seven, Russia sold Alaska to the United States.
The price was seven million dollars, about two cents for each acre.
People called it a foolish deal, until gold and oil were found there.

hook: Australia has the most wild camels in the world.
facts: In the eighteen hundreds, camels were brought to Australia to cross the desert.
When trucks and trains arrived, many camels were set free.
Today, hundreds of thousands roam wild, and Australia even sells camels to the Middle East.

hook: One Japanese island is ruled by rabbits.
facts: Okunoshima is a small island in Japan.
Hundreds of wild rabbits run free there and hop up to tourists for food.
During World War Two, the island hid a secret factory making poison gas.

hook: Nobody is allowed on one island because of snakes.
facts: Snake Island is off the coast of Brazil.
It is home to a rare and very deadly kind of golden snake.
There are so many that the government bans visitors, except some scientists.

hook: Diamonds can burn.
facts: Diamonds are made of pure carbon, just like coal.
If you heat one very hot with enough oxygen, it catches fire.
It burns away and turns into carbon dioxide, leaving nothing behind.

hook: A day on Mars is thirty-nine minutes longer.
facts: Mars spins a little slower than Earth.
One day on Mars lasts twenty-four hours and about thirty-nine minutes.
Engineers working on Mars missions lived on Mars time, and their days kept shifting.

hook: Mars is red because it is rusty.
facts: The ground on Mars is full of iron.
Over billions of years, the iron reacted with oxygen.
So the dust that covers the planet is rust, the same as an old nail.

hook: Saturn's rings are slowly disappearing.
facts: The rings are made of ice and rock.
Bits of the rings keep falling into Saturn, like rain.
Scientists think they could be gone in a few hundred million years.

hook: The gold on your finger came from dead stars.
facts: Gold cannot be made in normal stars.
It is made when two dead stars smash together in space.
So every gold ring on Earth was made in a cosmic crash, long before our planet existed.

hook: The Moon was made in a giant crash.
facts: Scientists think a planet the size of Mars hit the young Earth.
The crash threw huge amounts of melted rock into space.
The rock came together into a ball, and that ball became the Moon.

hook: Earth sent a music album into space.
facts: In nineteen seventy-seven, two Voyager spacecraft left Earth with a golden record.
It holds greetings in more than fifty languages, whale songs, and music.
It even has a rock and roll song, in case aliens find it.

hook: Stars twinkle, but planets do not.
facts: Stars are so far away they look like single points of light.
Moving air bends that tiny light back and forth, so it seems to flicker.
Planets are closer and look like small discs, so their light stays steady.

hook: Sunlight makes some people sneeze.
facts: About one person in four sneezes when they walk into bright light.
Scientists think the nerve signals for light and for sneezing get mixed.
It is passed down in families, and it is called the photic sneeze reflex.

hook: Your appendix may not be useless.
facts: For a long time, doctors said the appendix had no job.
Scientists now think it stores good gut bacteria.
After a bad stomach illness, those bacteria can come out and refill your gut.

hook: You breathe mostly through one nostril at a time.
facts: Your nose has two sides that take turns.
Every few hours, one side swells a little, and the other side opens up.
You almost never notice, but right now one nostril is working harder.

hook: Everyone with blue eyes shares one ancestor.
facts: Long ago, all humans had brown eyes.
Between six and ten thousand years ago, one person got a small change in a gene.
Scientists think everyone with blue eyes today comes from that one person.

hook: One fish lives inside a sea cucumber's bottom.
facts: The pearlfish is a thin, eel-like fish.
During the day, it hides inside the body of a sea cucumber.
It gets in through the back end, tail first.

hook: Male anglerfish melt into the female.
facts: In the deep sea, anglerfish rarely meet each other.
When a tiny male finds a female, he bites her and holds on.
Their bodies fuse together, and he lives on as part of her forever.

hook: Moths live in the fur of sloths.
facts: Sloths move so slowly that tiny plants grow in their fur.
Moths live there too, and lay eggs when the sloth climbs down to poop.
The moths help feed the plants, and the sloth may eat the plants as a snack.

hook: All clownfish are born male.
facts: Clownfish live in small groups inside sea anemones.
The biggest fish in the group is the only female.
When she dies, the biggest male turns into a female and takes her place.

hook: Bumblebees play with balls for fun.
facts: Scientists put small balls in a box with bumblebees.
The bees rolled the balls again and again, with no food as a reward.
Young bees did it the most, just like children playing.

hook: Giraffes hum at night.
facts: For a long time, people thought giraffes made almost no sounds.
Scientists recorded giraffes in zoos for hundreds of hours.
At night, they made a low humming sound, and nobody knows why.

hook: Zebra stripes confuse flies.
facts: Scientists put horses in coats with black and white stripes.
Flies flew toward them, but failed to land properly.
The stripes seem to confuse the flies, so zebras get far fewer bites.

hook: Cats meow mostly to talk to humans.
facts: Kittens meow to their mother when they need something.
Adult cats almost never meow to each other.
They keep meowing as adults mainly to get attention from people.

hook: A pigeon once saved two hundred soldiers.
facts: In World War One, almost two hundred American soldiers were trapped.
Their own army was shelling them by mistake.
A pigeon named Cher Ami flew through gunfire with a message, lost a leg, and won a medal.

hook: Butterflies drink the tears of turtles.
facts: In the Amazon, salt is hard to find for animals that eat plants.
Some butterflies land on the heads of river turtles.
They drink the turtles' tears to get the salt.

hook: One bird decorates its home to find love.
facts: Male bowerbirds build a little hut out of sticks.
Then they decorate it with flowers, shells, and bright objects, often all blue.
Females visit and choose the male with the best design.

hook: One fish can fill a bucket with slime.
facts: The hagfish lives on the ocean floor.
When attacked, it releases slime that grows fast in sea water.
In seconds it can fill a bucket, and it once covered an American highway after a truck crash.

hook: Electric eels are not eels.
facts: Electric eels look like eels, long and thin.
But they belong to a different group of fish, closer to carp and catfish.
They can give a shock strong enough to knock over a horse.

hook: Lego means play well.
facts: Lego was started by a Danish carpenter in the nineteen thirties.
He made the name from two Danish words, leg godt, which mean play well.
Later, he learned that lego in Latin can mean I put together.

hook: IKEA is a name made of initials.
facts: The founder started the company when he was just seventeen.
I and K come from his name, Ingvar Kamprad.
E and A come from the farm and the village where he grew up.

hook: Adidas and Puma were founded by angry brothers.
facts: Adi and Rudolf Dassler made shoes together in a small German town.
After a bitter fight, they split up and each started his own company.
The town was divided, and people looked at your shoes before talking to you.

hook: Lamborghini started out making tractors.
facts: Ferruccio Lamborghini got rich making farm tractors in Italy.
He owned a Ferrari and complained to Enzo Ferrari about its clutch.
The story says Ferrari told him to stick to tractors, so he built his own sports cars.

hook: Samsung started by selling dried fish.
facts: Samsung was founded in Korea in nineteen thirty-eight.
At first it sold dried fish, vegetables and noodles.
Today it makes phones, TVs, ships and even builds skyscrapers.

hook: Pepsi was sold to help your stomach.
facts: Pepsi was invented by a pharmacist in North Carolina.
He sold it as a drink to help with digestion.
The name likely comes from dyspepsia, the medical word for an upset stomach.

hook: The name of one famous spray means forty tries.
facts: In nineteen fifty-three, a small company tried to make a spray that pushes water away.
It failed again and again.
The fortieth formula worked, so they called it W D forty, for water displacement.

hook: Scrabble points came from a newspaper.
facts: The inventor of Scrabble wanted to know which letters are most common.
He counted the letters on the front page of The New York Times.
Common letters like E got one point, and rare ones like Q got ten.

hook: Barbie has a full name.
facts: Barbie was created by Ruth Handler in nineteen fifty-nine.
She named the doll after her daughter Barbara, and Ken after her son.
Barbie's full name is Barbara Millicent Roberts.

hook: Silly Putty was a failed war experiment.
facts: During World War Two, scientists tried to make fake rubber.
One mix bounced and stretched, but was useless for tires.
It became a toy instead, and astronauts even took it to space.

hook: Edison did not invent the light bulb.
facts: Many inventors made glowing bulbs before him.
Edison made one that lasted long enough to sell, and built a power system around it.
In Britain, Joseph Swan made a working bulb too, and the two men ended up in business together.

hook: The Ferris wheel was built to beat Paris.
facts: Paris had just shown off the Eiffel Tower at a world fair.
For the eighteen ninety-three fair in Chicago, America wanted something even better.
Engineer George Ferris built a giant wheel, with cars as big as buses.

hook: Volvo gave away the seat belt for free.
facts: In nineteen fifty-nine, a Volvo engineer invented the modern three point seat belt.
Volvo could have made a fortune from it.
Instead, it let every car maker use the design, because it saves lives.

hook: Windshield wipers were invented by a woman.
facts: In nineteen oh two, Mary Anderson rode a streetcar in New York in the snow.
The driver kept opening the window to clean the glass by hand.
She designed a blade you could move from inside, and it became the first windshield wiper.

hook: The dishwasher was invented by a rich woman.
facts: Josephine Cochrane loved hosting dinner parties in the eighteen eighties.
She was angry that her servants kept chipping her fine dishes.
So she designed a machine to wash them, and her company later became KitchenAid.

hook: Bulletproof vests come from a failed experiment.
facts: In nineteen sixty-five, chemist Stephanie Kwolek was working on a strong fiber for tires.
She made a cloudy liquid that others wanted to throw away.
She tested it anyway, and it became Kevlar, five times stronger than steel for its weight.

hook: The paper clip was a symbol of resistance.
facts: In World War Two, Germany occupied Norway.
Norwegians started wearing paper clips on their clothes.
It was a quiet sign that they stood together against the invaders.

hook: Pencils have never had lead in them.
facts: In the fifteen hundreds, a huge pile of black mineral was found in England.
People thought it was a kind of lead.
It was graphite, a form of carbon, but the name pencil lead never went away.

hook: Elevators were scary until one man cut the rope.
facts: Early elevators could fall if the rope broke.
In eighteen fifty-four, Elisha Otis stood on a platform high above a crowd in New York.
He had the rope cut, his safety brake caught it, and he shouted: all safe.

hook: A journalist invented the ballpoint pen.
facts: Laszlo Biro was a journalist in Hungary.
He noticed newspaper ink dried fast, but was too thick for a normal pen.
He used a tiny rolling ball at the tip, and in Britain pens are still called biros.

hook: Psycho shocked America with a flushing toilet.
facts: In nineteen sixty, Hollywood had strict rules about what could be shown.
A toilet on screen was seen as rude.
Hitchcock showed one flushing anyway, and it shocked audiences.

hook: Toy Story Two was almost deleted forever.
facts: During production, someone ran a computer command by mistake.
Woody, Buzz and most of the film started vanishing from the system.
It was saved because one worker had a copy at home, where she worked after having a baby.

hook: Godzilla's name means gorilla whale.
facts: The original Japanese name is Gojira.
It mixes the words for gorilla and whale.
The creators wanted a monster as strong as a gorilla and as big as a whale.

hook: ET was supposed to eat M and Ms.
facts: The film makers asked to use M and Ms to lure the alien.
The company said no.
They used Reese's Pieces instead, and sales of the candy jumped after the film.
